title: WHO grades of hearing loss (2021)
text: The World Report on Hearing grades hearing loss on the better-hearing ear's pure-tone average of 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz: normal below 20 dB HL; mild 20 to below 35; moderate 35 to below 50; moderately severe 50 to below 65; severe 65 to below 80; profound 80 to below 95; complete or total 95 dB HL or more.
source: World Health Organization. World report on hearing. Geneva: WHO

title: Unilateral hearing loss in the WHO scheme
text: WHO lists unilateral hearing loss as its own category: the better ear has a four-frequency average below 20 dB HL and the worse ear 35 dB HL or more. A person in this group may have no problem in quiet unless sound comes from the poorer side, but may have real difficulty following conversation.
source: Olusanya BO, Davis AC, Hoffman HJ. Bull World Health Organ 97(10):725–728. PMID 31656340

title: Hearing experience in quiet and in noise
text: Each WHO grade carries a plain description of what an adult usually experiences in a quiet room and in a noisy setting. These descriptions help when explaining results to clients and families, and link the audiometric grade to everyday activity and participation (ICF).
source: Olusanya BO, Davis AC, Hoffman HJ. Bull World Health Organ 97(10):725–728, Table 2. PMID 31656340

title: Why the WHO normal limit is now 20 dB HL
text: The 2021 scheme lowered the upper limit of normal hearing to below 20 dB HL (earlier WHO schemes used 25 dB HL) and added the 'complete or total' grade, so that mild losses that still affect conversation in noise are recognised.
source: Chadha S, Kamenov K, Cieza A. The world report on hearing, 2021. Bull World Health Organ 99(4):242. PMID 33953438

title: Pure-tone average
text: The four-frequency average (0.5, 1, 2, 4 kHz) is used for WHO grading. The three-frequency average (0.5, 1, 2 kHz) is still widely reported and relates closely to the speech reception threshold. Report which average you used.
source: World Health Organization. World report on hearing

title: No response at the audiometer limit
text: A no-response is plotted at the audiometer's maximum output with a downward arrow. The true threshold is poorer than that level, so an average that includes a no-response cannot be given as a number. Record the grade clinically, noting the limit.
source: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. Guidelines for audiometric symbols. ASHA 32(Suppl 2):25–30

title: ASHA audiometric symbols
text: Right ear air conduction: O unmasked, triangle masked. Left ear air conduction: X unmasked, square masked. Bone conduction: < and > unmasked, [ and ] masked, placed on the side of the frequency line for the ear tested. Air-conduction symbols are joined with lines; bone-conduction symbols are not joined.
source: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. Guidelines for audiometric symbols. ASHA 32(Suppl 2):25–30

title: Audiogram proportions
text: On a standard audiogram one octave on the frequency axis occupies the same distance as 20 dB on the hearing-level axis. Keeping this ratio stops the slope of a loss looking steeper or flatter than it is.
source: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. Guidelines for audiometric symbols. ASHA 32(Suppl 2):25–30

title: Air–bone gap and type of loss
text: A mean air–bone gap greater than 10 dB suggests a conductive component. With bone conduction within normal limits the loss is conductive; with bone conduction also elevated it is mixed. A gap of 10 dB or less with elevated thresholds suggests sensorineural loss. Confirm with masking, tympanometry and clinical findings.
source: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. Guidelines for manual pure-tone threshold audiometry

title: When to mask
text: Mask the non-test ear when the air-conduction threshold of the test ear could be heard by cross-hearing (difference from the non-test ear's bone conduction at or above interaural attenuation, about 40 dB with supra-aural earphones), and in bone conduction whenever an air–bone gap is present. Use the plateau method and record masked symbols.
source: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. Guidelines for manual pure-tone threshold audiometry

title: Bone-conduction test range
text: Bone conduction is usually tested from 250 to 4000 Hz. Output limits are lower than for air conduction, and responses at low frequencies and high levels may be felt rather than heard (vibrotactile). Note suspected vibrotactile responses.
source: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. Guidelines for manual pure-tone threshold audiometry

title: Threshold search steps
text: Thresholds are found with the modified Hughson–Westlake method: down 10 dB after each response, up 5 dB after each miss, and threshold is the lowest level heard on at least two of three ascending runs. Thresholds are therefore recorded in 5 dB steps.
source: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. Guidelines for manual pure-tone threshold audiometry
